title: Building a multi-asset crypto signal engine — 184 forward-tracked signals and now starting a clean LONG-only V1
author: Rare_Reference3909
selftext:
I've been building Nexyria, a quantitative crypto research project focused on generating and tracking trading signals automatically.



The system currently scans multiple assets and timeframes, generates signals, tracks TP/SL outcomes, and measures performance including estimated fees and slippage.



Current historical PRO dataset:



• 184 signals registered

• 179 closed

• 81 wins / 98 losses

• 45.25% win rate

• Profit Factor: 1.378

• Gross result: +37.00R

• Estimated result after modeled costs: +20.13R

• Net expectancy: +0.112R per trade

• Max drawdown: 12R



Instead of continuing to modify the same dataset, I've now frozen a new experimental version: PRO LONG Multi-Asset V1.



It currently monitors BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP, SUI and AAVE across 15m, 1h, 4h and 1d timeframes.



The new V1 starts with a completely clean forward record, so we'll be able to see whether the current logic actually holds up without mixing results from previous versions.



I'm also separating LONG and SHORT research rather than assuming that a profitable LONG model can simply be inverted. SHORT will have its own research and validation pipeline before being considered for the PRO system.



No claims of guaranteed profitability — the goal is to collect enough forward evidence to determine whether the edge survives costs and different market regimes.



I'm interested in feedback from people building systematic trading systems: what minimum forward sample would you want to see before considering a strategy genuinely interesting?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the long/short split is the best decision in the post, most people invert the long model and call it done.

on the sample question: a count is the wrong unit. 179 closed across six coins and four timeframes is a handful per cell, and worse, it is one regime. the forward record I would trust has to contain at least one stretch the logic hated, a chop month, a crash day, whatever your rules are worst at. until the record includes its own bad month you only know it works in the weather it was born in.

so my answer is not a number, it is a calendar. freeze V1, do not touch it, and wait for the market to hand you a bad month. then read it.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
That's a very useful point, especially the distinction between sample count and regime coverage.

That's exactly why V1 has now been frozen. I don't want to optimize it as new results arrive and accidentally turn forward testing into another training set.

I also like your point about waiting for the model to experience conditions where it performs badly. One thing I'm considering is tagging every forward signal by market regime and volatility, without changing the frozen strategy itself. That would let us evaluate not only N, PF and expectancy, but also where the edge survives or breaks down.

And yes, SHORT will remain a separate research pipeline rather than an inverted LONG model.

Thanks — this is exactly the kind of feedback I was looking for.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Tagging without changing the strategy is the right call. Two things will keep the tags honest:

* **Define the buckets now, before more results come in.** Fix the regime and volatility definitions (say, realized vol terciles plus a trend flag) and write them down. If you choose the buckets after seeing which ones look good, you've rebuilt a training set.
* **Assign the tag at signal time, using only data available then.** Regime labels computed retroactively with full-sample stats leak look-ahead into the tags.

Keep the number of buckets small. Slicing 400 trades into 12 cells leaves you comparing noise, and with enough slices something will look great by chance. Treat any "the edge only works in X" finding as a hypothesis to test on the next forward batch, not a conclusion.

One more tag worth adding is event context, meaning whether a signal fired near a scheduled macro print (CPI, FOMC) or a major crypto-specific event. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing with point-in-time timestamps, which makes that split easy without touching the frozen strategy.

It's also worth setting kill criteria up front, for example "if net expectancy is below 0 after N trades, or drawdown exceeds Y R, V1 is retired." It keeps you from rationalizing a losing stretch as a regime effect.

Good luck with V1. I'd be curious to see the interval on expectancy once you're past a few hundred trades.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
This is extremely useful. I agree that the regime definitions need to be frozen before seeing the outcomes, otherwise the monitoring layer itself can become another form of optimization.

I'll keep the number of buckets deliberately small and assign them point-in-time when each signal is generated.

I also like the idea of defining retirement criteria in advance. That would make it much harder to rationalize poor forward performance after the fact.

The event-context tag is interesting too, although I'd prefer to build or verify my own point-in-time event dataset rather than introduce another dependency at this stage.

Thanks again. This is helping shape the validation layer around V1 without touching the frozen strategy itself.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
That makes sense. Building your own keeps you in control of the definitions, which matters for a frozen setup. If you do build it, a few things tend to save headaches. Take scheduled release times from the official sources (BLS, the Fed calendar, exchange notices) and store each one with its local time zone and a UTC equivalent, since DST shifts will otherwise move your windows twice a year. Record when you first saw each entry, so a date that was only announced later doesn't get back-filled into the past. Keep revisions and unscheduled events as separate tags, because those are the ones most prone to leaking hindsight.

Once it's built, cross-checking a sample against a second source is a cheap way to catch mistakes. Cymetica's EventTrader could serve for that if you ever want a comparison. Otherwise, good luck with V1, and I'd enjoy seeing the update once you have a few hundred trades.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Thanks — especially for the point about recording when each event was first known. That is exactly the kind of detail we want to preserve to avoid accidentally introducing hindsight into the dataset.
To give a bit more context on the project, Nexyria already has a frozen multi-asset LONG V1 running in forward tracking across several assets and timeframes. Each signal is timestamped and tracked to its outcome without modifying the strategy based on incoming results. We are measuring metrics such as expectancy, profit factor and drawdown.
We have also decided to keep SHORT research separate from LONG rather than assuming the same logic can simply be inverted. The next layer we are preparing is precisely to tag the market regime and event context that existed at signal time, without changing the decisions of the frozen V1.
Your suggestion to store local time + UTC, a first-seen timestamp, revisions and unscheduled events separately fits very well with that approach. Using a second source purely as a quality-control check for the dataset also makes sense.
Once we have a substantially larger forward sample, I plan to share an update with the methodology and results — including the bad periods, not just the favorable ones.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Sounds like a solid setup, and I'd count sharing the bad periods as the most valuable part of the update. One small suggestion for when you publish: fix the sample cutoffs and the definitions of the regime and event tags in advance and include them in the write-up, so readers can see that nothing was tuned after the results came in. Looking forward to reading it once the sample is larger.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Agreed. I think predefining the sample cuts and regime/event labels before looking at the results will make the eventual update much more useful and auditable.
We’re also building a public-facing layer around Nexyria alongside the research system — a website plus FREE and PRO tools — but I’d rather finish that properly and keep collecting forward data before linking it here.
When both are ready, I’ll come back with the project, the frozen methodology, the predefined regime definitions and the forward results, including the weak periods. That should make it much easier to judge what is actually holding up out of sample.
Thanks again — your feedback has genuinely helped shape the validation layer.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: tagging by regime without touching the strategy is the right way round. frozen model, labelled outcomes.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Exactly. That’s the plan now: keep V1 untouched and build the regime/context layer around the forward results rather than feeding those results back into the strategy.
I also want the regime label to be assigned at signal time using only information available at that moment, so the analysis remains genuinely point-in-time.
Once the sample grows, it should give us a much clearer picture of whether the edge is robust or simply concentrated in a particular market environment.
Appreciate the feedback.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: point-in-time labels are the whole game there. if the regime tag gets recomputed later with hindsight, every losing trade quietly migrates into the bad-regime bucket and V1 looks better than it is.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Exactly. That’s the failure mode I want to avoid.
The regime label will be assigned and stored at signal time using only information available at that timestamp, and it won’t be recalculated later based on how the trade turned out.
The goal is to use regimes as an observational layer around the frozen V1, not as a way to reclassify losing trades after the fact. Once the forward sample is large enough, we can then test whether performance differences across regimes are actually persistent.
Appreciate you highlighting it — point-in-time integrity is going to be a hard requirement.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
that's the right discipline. store the inputs the label was computed from as well, not just the label, so a later fix to the classifier can't quietly rewrite history.

Quantradin is something I built for forward tests like this, free and paper only, at quantradin.com if a second ledger helps.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Good point. I was planning to persist the regime label and timestamp, but storing the exact classifier inputs alongside it makes the audit trail much stronger. That way even if the regime classifier changes later, the original forward record remains reproducible and immutable.
I’ll add that to the validation design. And thanks for mentioning Quantradin — I’ll take a look.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: sounds solid. a forward record you can reproduce after the classifier changes is the only kind worth trusting a year from now.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body: Agreed. That’s the standard I want to build toward: preserve enough point-in-time information that any forward signal can still be reconstructed months later, even if the classifier has evolved. Thanks for the useful feedback.
